# Repository instructions for Copilot

This is a demand forecasting project. Most changes here are made by the Copilot
cloud agent from issues that were generated from meeting transcripts, then
reviewed by both a human and a review agent. Follow these conventions so those
pull requests land cleanly.

## Setup

```bash
make install    # creates .venv and installs the project with dev extras
make check      # lint, notebook-output check, tests, notebook execution, eval gate
```

Individual targets: `make lint`, `make test`, `make notebooks`, `make backtest`,
`make gate`, `make data`, `make format`, `make strip`.

## Project layout

| Path | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| `src/forecasting/data.py` | Loading and chronological splitting |
| `src/forecasting/features.py` | Feature engineering |
| `src/forecasting/models/` | Forecaster implementations |
| `src/forecasting/registry.py` | Name to model factory mapping |
| `src/forecasting/evaluate.py` | Metrics and the rolling-origin backtest |
| `scripts/` | CLI entry points used by `make` and CI |
| `notebooks/` | EDA and model comparison |
| `eval/thresholds.yml` | The accuracy gate CI enforces |
| `tests/` | pytest suite |

## Rules

### Time series correctness comes first

- Never use a random train/test split. Use `train_test_split` or
  `rolling_origin_splits` from `forecasting.data`.
- Any feature derived from the target must be lagged by at least one step.
  `add_lag_features` and `add_rolling_features` already enforce this; keep it
  that way in anything new.
- Exogenous regressors are only legitimate if their future values are genuinely
  known at forecast time. `on_promotion` and `price` qualify. Anything computed
  from `units` does not.
- If you add a feature, add a test that proves it does not read the future.
  `tests/test_features.py` has the pattern: perturb the last target value and
  assert nothing earlier moves.
- The feature builders operate on **one series at a time** and call
  `validate_single_series` to enforce it. A bare `.shift()` over a multi-SKU
  frame does not produce a lag, it produces another SKU's value for the same
  date. To build features per SKU, loop over `select_sku` and call the builder
  once per series; keep the guard in place in anything new.

### Adding a model

1. Create `src/forecasting/models/<name>.py` with a class that subclasses
   `Forecaster` and implements `fit(history) -> self` and
   `predict(horizon) -> np.ndarray`.
2. Set a `name` class attribute.
3. Register it in `src/forecasting/registry.py`.
4. Export it from `src/forecasting/models/__init__.py`.
5. Add it to the `CHEAP_MODELS` parametrisation in `tests/test_models.py` if it
   fits in well under a second, otherwise give it its own test class marked
   `@pytest.mark.slow`.

Nothing else should need to change. If you find yourself editing `run_backtest.py`
or a notebook to special-case a model, the registry is being bypassed.

### Dependencies

- Do not add a runtime dependency to the default `dependencies` list without a
  clear reason. Heavy or slow-installing packages go in an optional extra under
  `[project.optional-dependencies]`, and CI installs the extra explicitly.
- `prophet` already has an extra defined. If you implement a Prophet forecaster,
  install it from that extra, import it lazily inside `fit`, and make the module
  import cleanly when Prophet is absent so the rest of the test suite still runs.

### The eval gate

- `eval/thresholds.yml` is a contract, not a suggestion. Do not raise a threshold
  to make a red build go green.
- If a change genuinely justifies new thresholds, say so explicitly in the pull
  request description with the before and after numbers.
- The champion model must beat the seasonal naive baseline. A model that only
  ties the baseline is a regression.

### Notebooks

- Notebooks must execute top to bottom with no manual steps and no network
  access. CI runs them with `pytest --nbmake`.
- Never commit notebook outputs. Run `make strip` before committing.
  `nbstripout --verify` runs in CI and will fail the build.
- Keep each notebook under about a minute of runtime. Heavy experiments belong
  in a script.

### Data

- `data/raw/sales.csv` is generated by `scripts/generate_data.py` with seed 7 and
  committed. Do not hand-edit it. `tests/test_scripts.py` verifies the committed
  file matches the generator.
- Changing the seed or the generating process changes every metric and will trip
  the eval gate. Only do it if that is the actual point of the change.

### Style

- Ruff with a 100 character line limit, configured in `pyproject.toml`. Run
  `make format`.
- Type hints on public functions. `from __future__ import annotations` at the top
  of modules.
- Docstrings explain why, not what. Skip the ones that just restate the signature.
- Comments only where the code genuinely needs clarification.

### Tests

- Every behavioural change needs a test. Every bug fix needs a test that fails
  before the fix.
- Test names describe the behaviour, not the function under test.
- Prefer hand-computed expected values over recomputing the implementation inside
  the test.

## Before you open the pull request

Run `make check`. If any part of it fails, fix it rather than skipping it. If
something is genuinely out of scope, say so in the pull request description
instead of leaving it silent.
